```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6, fig.height = 5)
```

```{r}
library(ethogramR)
```

ethogramR takes four inputs:

| Input | What it holds | Function |
|---|---|---|
| Observations | Scan and/or focal records (Ethogram app CSV layout) | `read_ethogram_csv()`, `as_obs()` |
| Ethogram | Behaviours, `type` (state/event), `class`, `directed`, `species_typical`, optional wild `reference` budget | `as_ethogram()` |
| Zones | `zone`, `area` (and `enclosure` if more than one) | `as_zones()` |
| Animals (optional) | `animal` plus attributes such as sex and age class | — |

## 1. Read the data

An Ethogram app export can be read directly. One file can hold scan and focal
sessions, so the analysis functions then ask which sampling method to use.

```{r}
f <- system.file("extdata", "ethogram_export_example.csv", package = "ethogramR")
obs <- read_ethogram_csv(f)
table(obs$sampling, obs$record_type)
scans <- obs[obs$sampling == "scan", ]
focal <- obs[obs$sampling == "focal", ]
```

Your own data in other layouts can be renamed on import, e.g.
`read_ethogram_csv("my.csv", map = c(animal = "ID", behaviour = "Behav", zone = "Area"))`.

The ethogram and zones are small tables you write once per group:

```{r}
example_ethogram
example_zones
```

`species_typical = FALSE` marks behaviours (e.g. pacing) that are left out of
diversity and reported as `prop_abnormal`. If the column is missing, any
behaviour whose name or class contains "abnormal" or "stereotyp" is treated as
not species-typical.

## 2. Activity budgets

```{r}
b <- behaviour_budget(scans, example_ethogram)
head(b)
```

For focal data, budgets are proportions of in-sight time
(`measure = "duration"`) or bout counts (`measure = "frequency"`);
`event_rates()` gives events per observed hour.

## 3. Species-typical behavioural diversity

```{r}
div <- behaviour_diversity(scans, example_ethogram, n_boot = 500, seed = 1)
div[c("animal", "richness", "prop_repertoire", "shannon", "shannon_lo", "shannon_hi",
      "evenness", "simpson", "prop_abnormal", "similarity_ref")]
```

* `richness` and `prop_repertoire`: how many species-typical behaviours were
  seen, and the share of the ethogram's repertoire this represents.
* `shannon` (H'), `evenness` (Pielou's J'), `simpson`: diversity and evenness
  of the budget.
* `evenness_repertoire`: H' / ln(repertoire size), which also penalises
  behaviours that never appear.
* `similarity_ref`: overlap with the wild `reference` budget (1 = identical).

Group-level values pool all animals:

```{r}
behaviour_diversity(focal, example_ethogram, by = NULL)
```

## 4. Enclosure use: spread of participation index

SPI uses the unequal-zone formula of Plowman (2003) when zone areas are given,
and Dickens' (1955) formula for equal zones. 0 means use in proportion to zone
size; 1 means only one zone was used.

```{r}
spi(scans, example_zones)
spi(focal, example_zones, by = NULL)   # focal: seconds in each zone
```

`zone_use()` shows which zones drive the score (Ivlev and Jacobs electivity:
positive = used more than its size predicts):

```{r}
zone_use(scans, example_zones, by = NULL)[c("zone", "observed", "expected", "ivlev", "jacobs")]
```

## 5. Social networks

**Association network** from co-occurrence in scans, by zone or by distance on
the enclosure map (app x/y are proportions, so give the map size in metres):

```{r}
am <- association_matrix(scans, method = "zone", index = "SRI")
am
am_d <- association_matrix(scans, method = "distance", max_dist = 10, map_size = c(60, 40))
```

For focal data, every animal's state is sampled every `focal_step` seconds
(`focal_to_scans()`) before the index is computed.

**Interaction network** from directed behaviours (actor in rows, recipient in
columns):

```{r}
im <- interaction_matrix(focal, example_ethogram)          # all directed behaviours
groom <- interaction_matrix(focal, behaviours = "Allogroom", measure = "duration")
groom
```

`rate = TRUE` divides by each actor's in-sight observation effort.

**Network metrics** and a plot:

```{r}
net <- network_metrics(am, attributes = example_animals)
net$network
net$nodes
plot_network(net, colour_by = "sex")
```

```{r}
plot_network(network_metrics(im, attributes = example_animals), colour_by = "community")
```

## 6. Everything at once

```{r}
res <- analyse_group(scans, example_ethogram, example_zones, animals = example_animals)
res
```

* Plowman, A. B. (2003). Applied Animal Behaviour Science 83: 331-336.
* Cairns, S. J. & Schwager, S. J. (1987). Animal Behaviour 35: 1454-1469.
* Hoppitt, W. J. E. & Farine, D. R. (2018). Animal Behaviour 136: 227-238.
* Miller, L. J. et al. (2020). Animals 10: 1211.
